2008 was, financially and politically speaking, a massive clusterfuck that takes a bit of time to fully explain. With regards to the usual response--that deregulation caused banks to become greedy and shortsighted--I have this to say. First, what deregulation? The years leading up to 2008 were by and large a period of increasing regulations, with laws such as the Sarbanes-Oxley Act being passed in droves in answer to fraud scandals. As the video describes, the only deregulation of note that occurred was a partial repeal of Glass-Steagall, namely the repeal of language that prevented a commercial bank and a financial bank from becoming part of the same holding company. This law however wouldn't have affected any of the banks involved in the financial crisis one way or the other, so you can't really claim that not repealing this law would have changed the situation. As for what actually caused the crash, there were several contributing factors. The first was the one that marks the start of every depression for the past century: The Fed instated an inflationary policy, keeping interest rates artificially low. Low interest rates cause more investments to be made. The reason for this is twofold: first, in a free market at least, low interest rates indicate low consumer time-preference: people are choosing to save money to spend later rather than spend it all now, which indicates future growth, and that promise of future growth signals to producers that they should invest in capital goods that allow them to produce more later, rather than spending that same money to maximize production in the short term. Second, even discounting this there's the simple fact that low interest rates incentivize more investment spending, because the "price" of taking out a loan is lower--you won't have to pay as much interest on it. When the Fed gets involved in interest rates, it separates interest rates from this idea of time-preference. So when interest rates become low, businesses see the signal, and respond to the incentive to invest, and buy more capital goods, because they expect future growth. Their businesses grow, they hire more people, and the economy enters the traditional "boom" phase of the business cycle--things are looking good. But the problem is, none of that future growth they are expecting is going to happen, because interest rates aren't low because consumer time-preference has gone down, they're low simply because the Fed has willed it to be. And when that expected growth never happens, you start to see a cluster of errors appear: firms collapse from insolvency, they have to fire people, foreclose on warehouses, sell off machinery, and what have you. This is the economic 'bust'--there was no real economic growth to account for the increase in capital spending, only the illusion of growth through money-printing and credit expansion. Were the Fed not involved in interest rates, and rates were set instead by the free market, this catastrophic clustering of errors would not occur. Businesses would still fail here and there of course, because the human mind isn't perfect and entrepreneurs make bad predictions even when they have good data, but you would no longer have the massive booms and busts of depressions.

This is what happened in 2008--artificially low interest rates made people invest a lot more than the market was able to sustain. But there were other factors in place which exacerbated the issue and made 2008 worse than other recessions. First, there was the Community Reinvestment Act, which allowed a large number of people who couldn't afford or have the credit for a mortgage apply for mortgages and become homeowners. These people couldn't in the slightest afford the mortgages they had, so default was inevitable--this adds another cluster of errors on top of the ones introduced by the Fed's credit expansion. This could have been made less of an issue if people were aware of the risk of the mortgages in which they were investing--but they couldn't, because extensive federal regulation made sure that there were only two ratings agencies in the securities market, as opposed to the large number that competition would bring. Because they had no incentive to compete, the quality of their services went down, and they didn't make an effort to give accurate predictions. Bribery--which can only reasonably be done if there are a small number of actors in a market--exacerbated this issue further.
